architecture.rule: Do not apply Onion Architecture or Clean Architecture to Django projects unless the project explicitly overrides this rule.

urls.rule:
urls.py files should only map routes to views or ViewSets.
Each app should own its urls.py, included from the project's root urls.py.

viewsets.rule:
ViewSets should validate requests and call services.
ViewSets should contain no business logic.

validation.rule: Validate request data with serializers instead of manual checks in views.
Use explicit serializer fields for responses so unlisted model fields are not leaked.

models.rule: Each domain database model should have its own Django app when the domain is sufficiently independent.

managers.rule: Use custom Django managers to encapsulate common and core database queries and table-level pre-filtering operations.

permissions_and_mixins.rule: Permission classes and mixins shared by views should live in their own files.

authorization.rule: For authorization, use Policy classes similar to the policy pattern used by Ruby on Rails, exposed to views through DRF permission classes.

error_handling.rule: Use a single custom DRF EXCEPTION_HANDLER as the global exception handler. Views and services should raise exceptions instead of building error responses.

authentication.rule: When user authentication exists, request.user should contain the authenticated user, set by Django's or DRF's authentication classes.

multi_tenancy.rule: When multi-tenancy exists, a middleware should set request.tenant with the current tenant information.

settings.rule: Split Django settings into multiple files.
Maintain separate development, production, and test settings.
Use a base settings layer for settings shared by multiple environments.

logging.rule: Configure the global logger through the LOGGING setting and get loggers with logging.getLogger(__name__).
